missions.title: Two cells
missions.goalText: Meet the plant cell and the animal cell.
hints: One cell has a thick wall around it.
The plant cell is the box-shaped one.

missions.title: Cell wall
missions.goalText: Find what the cell wall is made of.
hints: The fibres are long strands that cross over each other.
Cellulose fibres make up the thick wall itself.

missions.title: Cell membrane
missions.goalText: Find what controls what enters and leaves the cell.
hints: Proteins are the larger shapes sitting across the membrane.
Look for the shape with a passage through its middle.

missions.title: Nucleus
missions.goalText: Find the parts of the nucleus.
hints: The nucleolus is the dark ball inside the nucleus.
Look through the open wedge of the envelope.

missions.title: Ribosomes
hints: The protein chain comes out of the large subunit.
It is the beaded strand leaving the top of the ribosome.

missions.title: Endoplasmic reticulum
missions.goalText: Tell rough ER from smooth ER.
hints: Smooth ER has no dots on it.
It looks like a tangle of smooth tubes.

missions.title: Golgi apparatus
missions.goalText: Find out what the Golgi apparatus does.
hints: Think of a post office.
Vesicles carry its packages away.

missions.title: Lysosomes
missions.goalText: Find what is inside a lysosome.
hints: The enzymes are the small particles inside.
Look inside the open bag.

missions.title: Vacuoles
hints: It is the big, clear, pale blue sac.
Look in the plant cell.

missions.title: Mitochondria
missions.goalText: Find the parts of a mitochondrion.
hints: Look inside the opened mitochondrion.
The cristae are the shelves that fold in from the inner membrane.

missions.title: Chloroplasts
hints: Chloroplasts are green.
Look in the box-shaped plant cell.

missions.title: Recap
hints: Chloroplasts are only in plant cells.

cues.captionText: Welcome to the world of cells. Every living thing is made of cells.
This is a plant cell. A firm cell wall surrounds it, so it keeps a box-like shape.
This is an animal cell. It has no cell wall, only a soft cell membrane, so its shape is rounder.
Both cells are full of tiny parts called organelles. Each organelle has its own job.
See the orange, bean-shaped parts? They are mitochondria.
The plant cell has mitochondria too. Both cells need them.
A mitochondrion is the powerhouse of the cell. It releases energy from food so the cell can do its work.
A mitochondrion has two membranes. This is the outer membrane.
The inner membrane folds inwards again and again. These folds are called cristae.
The fluid inside the inner membrane is called the matrix.
Now look for the green, oval parts in the plant cell. They are chloroplasts.
The animal cell has no chloroplasts. Only plant cells have them.
A chloroplast holds a green pigment called chlorophyll. It uses sunlight to make food for the plant.
Like a mitochondrion, it has an outer membrane and an inner membrane.
Inside are stacks of flat discs called thylakoids. These stacks are the grana.
The fluid around the grana is called the stroma.
Now let's go back to both cells.
Let's compare. Mitochondria are in both cells. Chloroplasts are only in plant cells.
Plants make their own food using sunlight, so they need chloroplasts. Every cell needs energy, so every cell has mitochondria.
The correct answer is: Mitochondrion. Mitochondria release energy from food, so they are called the powerhouse of the cell.
The correct answer is: Folds of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion. Cristae are the folds of a mitochondrion's inner membrane. The fluid inside is the matrix.
The correct answer is: Plant cells only. Chloroplasts are found in plant cells. Animal cells do not have them.
The correct answer is: Stacks of thylakoids. The grana are stacks of thylakoids. The fluid around them is the stroma.
The correct answer is: An animal cell. Plant cells have a cell wall, and green plant cells have chloroplasts. A cell with neither is an animal cell.
The correct answer is: To make food using sunlight. Chloroplasts use sunlight to make food. Mitochondria release energy from that food.
Only the plant cell has this thick outer layer. It is the cell wall.
The wall is made mostly of cellulose. Long cellulose fibres cross over each other, like threads in cloth.
Between two neighbouring plant cells is the middle lamella. It glues the cells together.
Tiny channels called plasmodesmata pass through the walls, so neighbouring cells can share materials.
The wall gives the plant cell its shape and strength, and protects it. Water and dissolved substances pass through it freely.
Every cell has a cell membrane. In the animal cell it is the outer boundary.
In the plant cell, the membrane lies just inside the cell wall.
Up close, the membrane is two layers of phospholipids, called a lipid bilayer.
Their water-loving heads face outwards. Their water-hating fatty tails point into the middle.
Proteins sit in the membrane. Some form channels that let chosen substances in and out.
So the membrane is selectively permeable. It lets some substances through and keeps others out.
This large, round organelle is the nucleus. It is the control centre of the cell.
The plant cell has a nucleus too, pushed to one side by its big vacuole.
The nucleus is wrapped in a double membrane called the nuclear envelope.
Pores in the envelope let messages and materials pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
Inside is chromatin, made of DNA. DNA carries the instructions for building and running the cell.
The dark, dense body is the nucleolus. It makes ribosomes.
These tiny dark dots are ribosomes. There are thousands in every cell.
Plant cells are full of them too. Some float free in the cytoplasm, and others sit on the endoplasmic reticulum.
A ribosome has two parts: a large subunit and a small subunit.
Between them runs a message from the nucleus, called messenger RNA.
The ribosome reads the message and joins building blocks into a chain. That chain becomes a protein.
Around the nucleus is a folded network of membranes: the endoplasmic reticulum, or ER.
Rough ER is covered in ribosomes. It carries the proteins they make through the cell.
Smooth ER has no ribosomes. It makes fats, called lipids, and helps remove harmful substances.
Together they form a network of channels, a transport system inside the cell.
This stack of flattened sacs is the Golgi apparatus.
Each flat sac is called a cisterna. Proteins from the ER arrive at one side of the stack.
The Golgi changes, sorts and packs them, like the post office of the cell.
Packed materials leave in small bubbles called vesicles, to be sent inside or outside the cell.
These small round sacs are lysosomes. They are made by the Golgi apparatus.
A lysosome is a membrane bag full of digestive enzymes.
The enzymes break down waste, worn-out parts of the cell, and germs that get in.
Its membrane keeps the enzymes inside, so they do not digest the rest of the cell.
If the cell is badly damaged, lysosomes may burst and digest it. So they are called suicide bags.
The plant cell has one large central vacuole. It can fill most of the cell.
Animal cells have small vacuoles, and only a few.
The vacuole is filled with cell sap: water with dissolved sugars, salts and other substances.
Its membrane is called the tonoplast.
A full vacuole presses outwards against the wall. That keeps the plant cell firm, so plants stand upright.
Now look at both cells again.
Both cells have a membrane, a nucleus, ribosomes, ER, a Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and mitochondria. Only the plant cell has a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.
The correct answer is: Cellulose. The plant cell wall is made mainly of cellulose. Its long fibres make the wall strong.
The correct answer is: Its rigid cell wall supports it. The rigid cell wall supports the plant cell and gives it a fixed, box-like shape.
The correct answer is: It lets some substances pass and stops others. The cell membrane lets some substances pass and keeps others out, so it is selectively permeable.
The correct answer is: Lipids and proteins. The cell membrane is a double layer of lipids (phospholipids) with proteins set into it.
The correct answer is: It holds the DNA that directs the cell's work. The nucleus holds the DNA, the instructions that direct everything the cell does.
The correct answer is: Let materials pass in and out of the nucleus. Nuclear pores are openings in the envelope that let materials and messages pass in and out of the nucleus.
The correct answer is: Proteins. Ribosomes read the message from the nucleus and build proteins.
The correct answer is: The nucleolus. The nucleolus, inside the nucleus, makes ribosomes.
The correct answer is: Ribosomes attached to it. Rough ER is studded with ribosomes, which make it look rough.
The correct answer is: Making lipids (fats). Smooth ER makes lipids (fats) and helps remove harmful substances.
The correct answer is: Vesicles. Vesicles are small membrane bubbles that carry the packed materials away.
The correct answer is: The rough ER. Proteins made on the rough ER travel to the Golgi apparatus to be packed.
The correct answer is: Their enzymes can digest the cell itself. If the cell is damaged, lysosomes can burst and their enzymes digest the cell itself.
The correct answer is: Its membrane. The lysosome's membrane keeps its digestive enzymes inside.
The correct answer is: Cell sap. The central vacuole is filled with cell sap: water with dissolved sugars and salts.
The correct answer is: It keeps the cell firm, so the plant stands upright. A full vacuole presses against the cell wall and keeps the cell firm, so the plant stands upright.
